doc.title: Joel Dorn interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 13, 2007

title: Leaving Atlantic after the hits
summary: Dorn explains his exit from Atlantic: his own behavior, interference after the Flack, Midler and Hathaway hits, friction with Wexler and Ahmet, and Nesuhi's absence.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Quitting the band: why sidemen left

blocks.x: Let me go backwards a little bit. Your employment with Atlantic came to an end?

Well first of all I was a wise ass kid and I was high most of the time so I didn’t exactly comport myself the way somebody should. Secondly I had had a lot of success and nobody bothered with me while I was making jazz records for Nesuhi. When I started to get hits with Flack and Midler and Donny Hathaway and people like that I had too much help. I wasn’t in the mood for that shit you know, to be honest with you. I got in hassles with Wexler, I got in hassles with Ahmet, you know. I just wanted to be — Nesuhi put me off in a corner. I could do what I wanted.
You mean they started telling you how to —

Pretty much, and also we didn’t get along personally. So it was weird. Had I been a better politician I might have navigated those waters better, but I wouldn’t change the records I was making. You know, and I work a certain way. It’s not that it’s good or bad or better or worse or anything, it’s the only way I know how. And you know I would mix a record and someone would say make this louder, make this softer. I’d do a song and someone would say don’t — I wasn’t hired on that basis and plus, Atlantic had gone from becoming the greatest record label in the history of record labels ever, to a big record company. So it wasn’t that small boutique shop where guys like me could do what they wanted because that’s what it was. All three guys who owned the company were producers. And Arif, Tom Dowd and I, me being the low man on that totem pole, were the non-owners who produced for the label. And I became successful. Listen, I’m going to tell you the truth, I did not handle success well. But also, I was making records that sold. Those records, I live off of those records. So they still sell. So I was doing something right. I was just a big mouth kid, you know, so it didn’t work well. And the Atlantic Records I left was not the Atlantic Records that I came to and Nesuhi was gone, he was in Europe, so I had nobody to protect me anymore.
Were you there when they signed Aretha?
I came just after Aretha’s first album.

And that was like the heyday of Atlantic R&B. Because they had Aretha, they had Wilson Pickett, they had the whole Memphis thing with Otis and Sam & Dave and you know, that crew. So the place was insane.
